reason: The sources robustly support the story with over 15 multi-source claims covering Mariner 10's historic gravity assist, in-flight crises, solar sailing, and planetary discoveries.
story: In 1973, NASA launched Mariner 10 on a shoestring budget to attempt what seemed impossible: reaching Mercury using a gravitational slingshot past Venus. No mission had ever pulled off an interplanetary gravity assist. On its way, the probe suffered relentless breakdowns. Its camera heaters failed, the onboard computer repeatedly reset, and shiny flakes of peeling paint confused the star-tracker into mistaking paint specks for the guide star Canopus. When attitude control gas began running critically low, engineers improvised a historic first, angling the solar panels to sail on the pressure of sunlight itself. The gambit paid off. Venus pulled Mariner 10 onto a trajectory that slung it past Mercury not once, but three times. Its cameras beamed back images of a heavily cratered, Moon-like world and detected an unexpected intrinsic magnetic field. Running entirely out of fuel, Mariner 10 went silent in 1975, left orbiting the Sun forever.
angle: When its thruster gas began running out on the way to Mercury, Mariner 10 survived by angling its solar panels into the solar wind, becoming the first spacecraft to navigate by sailing on sunlight.

claims.claim: Mariner 10 launched from Florida on November 3, 1973.
Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft to visit the planet Mercury.
Mariner 10 was the first mission to explore two planets during a single voyage.
Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft to use a planetary gravity assist to redirect its trajectory toward another planet.
Shortly after launch, heaters for Mariner 10's television cameras failed to turn on, threatening the imaging equipment with extreme cold.
The probe's star-tracker repeatedly lost lock on the guide star Canopus after mistaking bright flakes of shedding paint for the star.
Mariner 10 used solar radiation pressure against its solar panels and antenna as an active method of attitude control.
Mariner 10 made its closest approach to Venus on February 5, 1974, skimming within about 5,800 kilometers.
During its Venus encounter, Mariner 10 transmitted more than 4,000 photographs back to Earth.
Ultraviolet photography from Mariner 10 revealed dynamic cloud structures on Venus that were virtually invisible in visible light.
Mariner 10 completed three separate flybys of Mercury between 1974 and 1975.
The first flyby of Mercury occurred on March 29, 1974.
The second flyby of Mercury took place on September 21, 1974.
The third flyby of Mercury on March 16, 1975, was the closest, passing approximately 200 miles (327 kilometers) above the surface.
Photographs sent back by Mariner 10 revealed that Mercury possesses a heavily cratered, Moon-like surface.
Mariner 10's instruments revealed that Mercury has an intrinsic magnetic field.
Mariner 10 detected a tenuous atmosphere around Mercury composed primarily of helium.
Mission controllers sent commands to shut down Mariner 10's transmitter on March 24, 1975, after its attitude control gas was exhausted.
The United States Postal Service issued a commemorative postage stamp in 1975 honoring Mariner 10.

disputed: Originator of the gravity assist trajectory: S1 attributes the calculations for the resonant Mercury return orbit to Giuseppe Colombo, while S4 highlights Michael A. Minovitch's pioneering computational work solving the restricted three-body problem for gravity-assisted interplanetary travel. A script should attribute both contributions appropriately.

Magnetic field characterization: S2 and S3 characterize Mercury's magnetic field as weak or small (roughly 1/60th of Earth's), while S4 terms it 'fairly strong' relative to prior expectations of an inactive core. A script should simply state that Mercury possesses an unexpected intrinsic magnetic field.
